item.title: Gitea CVE-2026-20896 Probing, Rocket.Chat File Exposure, and Bandai Channel Attack
item.content:encoded:
Threat Actors Probe Gitea Docker Flaw CVE-2026-20896 13 Days After Disclosure — Must Read

Threat actors have begun probing a critical Gitea Docker image flaw, CVE-2026-20896, just 13 days after disclosure. Users should upgrade to Gitea 1.26.3 or later because the bug can let unauthenticated attackers impersonate users, including admins, when reverse-proxy authentication is misconfigured.

  • Threat actors have been observed attempting to exploit CVE-2026-20896, a critical flaw in Gitea Docker images, according to Sysdig.
  • CVE-2026-20896 has a CVSS score of 9.8 and allows unauthenticated internet clients to gain elevated access because Gitea trusts the X-WEBAUTH-USER header from any source IP address.
  • Security researcher Ali Mustafa said the issue stems from Gitea Docker images shipping an app.ini template that hard-codes REVERSE_PROXY_TRUSTED_PROXIES = * by default.
  • The vulnerability affects Gitea Docker image versions before and including 1.26.2 and was fixed in version 1.26.3 by removing the wildcard and making reverse-proxy authentication opt-in.
  • Sysdig said it detected the first in-the-wild exploitation attempt 13 days after public disclosure, with activity so far limited to initial investigation by the threat actor.

Predicting MongoDB ObjectId() continuously in Rocket.Chat — Should Read

Rocket.Chat had an unauthenticated file access flaw where attackers could use a valid Livechat room token to retrieve arbitrary uploaded files if they knew the file ID. Because MongoDB ObjectId values are predictable once an attacker can generate a probe ID, the researchers showed they could continuously discover and leak uploaded files until patched versions fixed the access-control check.

  • Aikido researchers found that an unauthenticated Rocket.Chat user could access uploaded files if they knew the file ID, and they reported the issue through HackerOne on April 21.
  • Rocket.Chat stored files from authenticated channels and unauthenticated Livechat in the same `/file-upload/{fileId}` location, but did not verify that the requested file belonged to the room used for access authorization.
  • The researchers used the Livechat feature to create an anonymous room and token, then supplied that room ID and token while requesting an arbitrary file ID to retrieve private file contents.
  • Because Rocket.Chat generated file IDs with MongoDB `ObjectId()`, the researchers showed that a probe upload could reveal the timestamp, static random value, and counter needed to predict other file IDs generated by the application.
  • Rocket.Chat fixed the issue in versions 8.5.1, 8.4.4, 8.3.6, 8.2.6, 8.1.6, 8.0.7, 7.13.9, and 7.10.13 by verifying that the requested file matches the specified room ID.

Japanese teen arrested over cyberattack that disrupted anime streaming service — May Read

Tokyo police arrested a 15-year-old suspected of exploiting a Bandai Channel server flaw and using a ChatGPT-assisted program to fraudulently cancel more than 46,000 anime streaming subscriptions. The attack forced the service offline for over a month while systems were repaired and subscribers refunded.

  • Tokyo police arrested a 15-year-old high school student suspected of carrying out cyberattacks against the Bandai Channel anime streaming service.
  • Police said the student allegedly exploited a server flaw to fraudulently cancel more than 46,000 user subscriptions.
  • Police said the teenager analyzed the service’s network traffic and used ChatGPT to develop a malicious program that automated the attacks.
  • The disruption forced Bandai Channel’s operator to suspend the platform for more than a month while it repaired systems and refunded affected subscribers.
  • Police said the suspect continued unauthorized account cancellations by repeatedly changing his IP address after the company blocked his access.

NDR Essentials: Stop Chasing Alerts, Start Hunting Adversaries — Optional

The article argues that Network Detection and Response should move security teams beyond reacting to endless alerts and toward proactively hunting adversary behavior across the network. The key takeaway is to focus on understanding attacker activity and intent, not just triaging isolated detections.

  • The article is titled “NDR Essentials: Stop Chasing Alerts, Start Hunting Adversaries.”
  • The article frames Network Detection and Response around moving away from chasing alerts.
  • The article emphasizes hunting adversaries as the preferred focus for network defense.

Software Is Now Written at the Speed of Thought. Security Isn't. — Optional

Generative AI and “vibe coding” are making software creation dramatically faster and accessible to non-developers, but they also risk producing insecure code, shadow applications, and unmanaged identities. Organizations need security practices like code review, threat modeling, least privilege, and AI governance to keep pace with AI-driven development.

  • The article describes software development as evolving from Waterfall to Agile, DevOps, generative AI, and Vibe Coding, with each stage reducing the friction between an idea and a deployable solution.
  • Vibe Coding allows a user, who is not necessarily a developer, to describe a desired application in plain English while AI generates and refines the application through conversation.
  • The article states that AI-generated code can contain vulnerabilities, architectural flaws, licensing issues, privilege escalation vulnerabilities, and compliance concerns even when the application appears to work correctly.
  • Traditional secure software engineering practices such as threat modeling, code review, vulnerability testing, identity security, least privilege, and governance controls remain essential before production deployment.
  • The author argues that cybersecurity best practices must evolve as quickly as AI-driven software creation so trust can be established in software built at the speed of thought.
